---
title: "Sorting messages by purpose"
subtitle: "Intent prediction and label design"
description: "Learn how intent classification routes messages and why the label schema controls what the system can do."
categories: [classification, intent classification, workforce research]
---

Luis manages the shared inbox while the front desk is closed. One message asks
for a password reset. Another asks whether a class accepts GED applicants. A
third reports a suspicious recruiter.

Routing the message is useful only if the label matches a real next step. A
worker can reset access, read application status, answer eligibility questions,
record a problem, or return a call. The label set does not describe actions
outside that list.

::: {.callout-note}
The Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and its training flyer are fictional
teaching materials.
:::

A dataset written by the classifier's author cannot establish whether the
method works generally. This lesson demonstrates calculations with the invented
inbox. It does not give an estimate of intake-system performance for real residents.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain intent classification in plain language.
- fit a small multi-class text model.
- examine multi-class probability output.
- find messages that need more than one routing label.
- explain why coarser taxonomies can make accuracy look better.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load the intent labels

An **intent** is what the sender wants the system to do. Each message in this
fixed teaching dataset has exactly one recorded intent, even when a person
might find several.

readr reads the file, while dplyr and tidyr reshape results. purrr selects
probability columns, and stringr evaluates simple rules. tidymodels,
textrecipes, and glmnet fit the model.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidymodels)
library(textrecipes)
library(glmnet)

inbox <- read_csv(
  "data/riverton/riverton-inbox.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    message_id = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    is_spam = col_logical(),
    intent = col_character(),
    author_note = col_character()
  )
) |>
  mutate(intent = factor(intent))

intent_counts <- inbox |>
  count(intent, name = "messages")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  intent_counts,
  col.names = c("Recorded intent", "Messages"),
  caption = "Intent labels in the invented inbox",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  all(c(
    "readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "tidyr", "purrr", "stringr",
    "ggplot2", "tidymodels", "textrecipes", "glmnet"
  ) %in% loadedNamespaces()),
  identical(nrow(inbox), 60L),
  identical(
    as.character(intent_counts$intent),
    c(
      "ask_eligibility",
      "check_status",
      "report_problem",
      "request_callback",
      "reset_access"
    )
  ),
  identical(intent_counts$messages, c(12L, 13L, 13L, 11L, 11L))
)
```

The label schema states the distinctions that the Lab can use. If staff cannot
act on a distinction, adding its label creates disagreement without improving
service.

## Fit a multi-class model

**Multi-class classification** chooses one label from more than two possible
labels. The seed before this fit is 5002. The model demonstrates the
calculations for a multi-class prediction.

```{r}
intent_recipe <- recipe(intent ~ text, data = inbox) |>
  step_tokenize(text) |>
  step_tokenfilter(text, max_tokens = 100) |>
  step_tfidf(text)

mechanics_rows <- inbox

intent_model <- multinom_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(5002)
intent_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(intent_recipe) |>
  add_model(intent_model) |>
  # The lesson reports nothing performance-related from these rows; it shows the
  # shape of a multi-class fit and states plainly why it scores nothing.
  fit(data = mechanics_rows) # resubstitution-ok: no score is reported

intent_predictions <- mechanics_rows |>
  select(message_id, text, intent) |>
  bind_cols(predict(intent_fit, mechanics_rows, type = "prob")) |>
  bind_cols(predict(intent_fit, mechanics_rows))

probability_columns <- names(intent_predictions) |>
  keep(\(column) str_starts(column, ".pred_") & column != ".pred_class")

probability_check <- intent_predictions |>
  transmute(
    message_id,
    probability_sum = rowSums(pick(all_of(probability_columns)))
  )

probability_display <- intent_predictions |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  select(message_id, all_of(probability_columns)) |>
  rename_with(
    \(column) str_remove(column, "^\\.pred_"),
    all_of(probability_columns)
  )

predicted_distribution <- intent_predictions |>
  count(.pred_class, name = "messages") |>
  arrange(.pred_class)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  probability_display |>
    mutate(across(-message_id, \(value) round(value, 3))),
  col.names = c(
    "Message",
    "Ask eligibility",
    "Read application status",
    "Report problem",
    "Request callback",
    "Reset access"
  ),
  caption = "Five class probabilities for three fitted-row examples",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  predicted_distribution,
  col.names = c("Predicted intent", "Messages"),
  caption = "Predicted-class distribution from the fitted multi-class model",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(intent_predictions), 60L),
  identical(length(levels(inbox$intent)), 5L),
  identical(length(probability_columns), 5L),
  all(abs(probability_check$probability_sum - 1) < 0.0000001),
  identical(nrow(probability_display), 3L),
  all(
    abs(
      rowSums(select(probability_display, -message_id)) - 1
    ) < 0.0000001
  ),
  identical(sum(predicted_distribution$messages), 60L),
  identical(
    as.character(predicted_distribution$.pred_class),
    c(
      "ask_eligibility",
      "check_status",
      "report_problem",
      "request_callback",
      "reset_access"
    )
  )
)
```

The fitted model has five classes. It returns five probabilities per message,
one per class, with a row sum of 1. The model predicts the same 60 rows it uses
for fitting. The table therefore demonstrates output structure rather than
performance. This lesson reports no performance score.

The classifier's author also wrote all 60 messages. A score on those messages
would describe this fixture rather than the method. Independent evaluation
requires messages from other authors and labels from reviewers who did not
build the model. It also requires a holdout set excluded from fitting.

## Find gaps in the taxonomy

A **taxonomy** specifies the labels and the rules for choosing them. Label
design can be harder than model fitting. If the taxonomy does not match the
work, accurate label predictions can still send messages to the wrong service.

```{r}
boundary_messages <- inbox |>
  filter(message_id %in% c("M034", "M055", "M044")) |>
  mutate(
    other_plausible_action = case_when(
      message_id == "M034" ~ "ask_eligibility or fraud review",
      message_id == "M055" ~ "ask_eligibility or fraud review",
      message_id == "M044" ~ "none without the missing request"
    ),
    why_it_strains_the_schema = case_when(
      message_id == "M034" ~
        "reports a suspicious listing but also mentions training and bank access",
      message_id == "M055" ~
        "asks whether an offer is real and reports a recruiter asking for ID",
      message_id == "M044" ~
        "gives call instructions without a full service request"
    )
  ) |>
  select(message_id, intent, other_plausible_action, why_it_strains_the_schema, text)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  boundary_messages,
  col.names = c(
    "Message",
    "Recorded intent",
    "Other plausible action",
    "Why one label is hard",
    "Text"
  ),
  caption = "Boundary cases for the intent taxonomy",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(boundary_messages$message_id, c("M034", "M044", "M055")),
  identical(
    as.character(boundary_messages$intent),
    c("report_problem", "request_callback", "report_problem")
  ),
  identical(
    boundary_messages$other_plausible_action,
    c(
      "ask_eligibility or fraud review",
      "none without the missing request",
      "ask_eligibility or fraud review"
    )
  ),
  all(str_length(boundary_messages$why_it_strains_the_schema) > 40L)
)
```

Messages M034 and M055 genuinely fit two actions. A staff member may both record
a problem and answer whether the offer is safe. If the Lab has a separate queue for fraud
checks, these two messages should probably go there. If it does not, the
worker must choose the nearest available label and record the information that
the label omits.

M044 fits none of the main service questions by itself. It gives a call
preference without the reason for the call. An intake system needs the missing
purpose before it can route the message. Lesson 11, "Working with several
annotators," explains why multiple reviewers should examine boundary cases
before choosing reference labels.

An `other` label covers messages that the designer did not anticipate. Staff
must examine those messages to find new service needs.

## Broader labels can increase measured accuracy

Combining intents into broader queues can increase the score for unchanged
predictions. The scoring task becomes easier without better classification.
This lesson does not compute that score. A rule fitted to these same 60
messages would provide another resubstitution result, a score calculated on its
training examples.

Broader categories may be appropriate when the organization cannot act on finer
distinctions. A report must not present the resulting increase in accuracy as
better understanding.

## What to remember

- Intent classification routes text by what the sender wants.
- The intent list must match actions the system can take.
- Probability output shows the shape of a multi-class prediction, not its quality.
- Boundary cases need human adjudication and clearer instructions.
- Coarser categories can raise measured accuracy by making the task easier.
